title: #56 Try These Four Different Ways of Going Through the Answers
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton critiques the default routine of reviewing independent-practice answers by projecting or modelling them while students tick and correct in a different-coloured pen, arguing this format gives little real evidence of participation or understanding. He offers four alternative techniques he has observed or developed. "Book-to-Board" has students copy a specific answer (or a single working step) from their exercise books onto mini-whiteboards on a 3-2-1 countdown, giving the teacher an instant whole-class read on a targeted question. "The Tick Trick," borrowed from Adam Boxer, allocates ticks for specific features of a good answer, forcing attention onto the working rather than just the final answer. "Cold Call Bounce" has one student give the first step of a solution and then "bounces" the response to another student to repeat, reflect on, or continue it, keeping the rest of the class listening since anyone could be picked next. "Call and Respond" is a fast whole-class chant-style technique reserved for short answers, useful when speed and inclusivity matter more than depth. Barton frames all four as more reliable diagnostic tools than a green-pen self-correction routine, since each increases either participation or the granularity of the data a teacher collects.
points: Barton's core critique is that projecting answers for students to self-mark in a different colour pen gives teachers almost no real data on whole-class understanding or participation.
"Book-to-Board" turns a single targeted question (or even just one working step) into a whole-class 3-2-1 check, letting a teacher diagnose exactly where understanding breaks down.

"The Tick Trick" (from Adam Boxer) allocates credit for specific components of a good answer -- units, layout, a written operation -- which redirects student attention to their working, not just their final answer.
"Cold Call Bounce" sustains listening across the class by passing one answer through multiple students to repeat, reflect on, or extend, rather than letting attention lapse after the first response.
quotes: I have written previously about why I think this approach does not work. But if we are not going to review the answers to independent practice in this way, then what are we going to do?

Ask students to copy their final answer for one of those questions from their books to their mini-whiteboards and show you in 3, 2, 1. This will immediately give you a sense of whole-class participation and understanding for that question.
When going through the answer to a question, you allocate ticks for specific things you want to see in students’ answers.

Cold Call one student to say the first step in the solution, then bounce it to another student to either repeat what the first student just said (a check for listening), to reflect on what they just said (a check for listening and a check of understanding), or to say the next step in the solution (a check for understanding).
Call and Respond is quicker than getting students to write their answers on mini-whiteboards, more inclusive than Cold Call, and students also love it.

Using one or more of these techniques when going through answers should help drive up the participation ratio and give you a more reliable sense of your students’ understanding than asking students to correct with a green pen will do.
